messages.subject: How is effort Incorporated
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I've been having a great time running my models in oSCR. It's super nice how I can have traps on/off in order to incorporate uneven sampling effort. I was just wondering if there was an explanation anywhere that talks about the mechanism behind how oSCR incorporates effort? Thanks!

messages.subject: Re: [oscr] How is effort Incorporated
messages.body_plain:
Glad to hear you are enjoying yourself 🙂

The trap operation matrix is provided as a binary matrix (0=off, 1=off). All oSCR does is multiply the probability of any individual-by-trap-by-occassion observation by the trap operation matrix entry for that trap-occassion. In this way, only observations in closed traps are impossible (prob=0) and therefore don't contribute to the likelihood or estimation.

Hope that is helpful?

messages.subject: Trap availability approach
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Along similar lines to the question asked earlier today, I am trying to figure out the best way to approach model setup for years of data where we have no information on trap availability. This is specifically for very trap happy foxes that are likely to have multiple traps in their home range that they can access.

Over our ~30 year dataset, we have some years with specific trap-night availability (great), some years with only the proportion of trap-nights available across all traps in a grid (not great), and some years with no information on availability at all (oh no). We are using yearly sessions, with grids (+ buffers) within a year aggregated into one state-space.

We have been debating the best way to deal with this inconsistency, with a couple ideas:

1. For years with only grid-level availability, randomly assign 'unavailable' trap-nights across non-capture trap-nights within each grid, based on the proportion of available trap-nights.
2. Ignore availability altogether, leaving all non-capture nights as 'available' (either for all years or only years with no information)

But generally we are having trouble wrapping our heads around how these approaches will impact the detection probability estimates and overall density estimates. Will it change the predicted activity center locations or population size estimates? Would changing the availability approach between years have unexpected effects? I'd love to get your thoughts on possible approaches or any considerations we should think about.

Thanks in advance for any insights you can provide!

Kirby Mills

messages.subject: Question about oSCR minimum recaptures
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone.

I would like ask for a bit of your wisdom here.

I applied oSCR to fit this multisession model to calculate population density of a very elusive felid. Set the encounter dataframe, trap dataframe, data function (data2oscr()), calculated sigma from 1/2 of the mmdm and set a buffer (3.5*sigma) for the Space State Dataframe.

(m1 <- oSCR.fit(model = list(D~1,         p0~session,  sig~1),            sl.sf, sl.ss)

Data comes from camera trap deployment. 83 location, 2 sessions, 17 captures, and 9 recaptures (One individual even 4 recaptures). Occasion length is 5 days.

 As expected the population estimates are not very robust. But my question is, Is there any specific lower limit for the number of recaptures below which SECR estimates become unreliable? The final estimates relate quite nicely to the actual population size.

Here are my estimates after backtransforming.

estimate                se                     lwr                    upr                Session
1 0.00919712      0.00437194     0.003622576   0.02334996       1

per Km2

The standard error is quite high, but does that automatically invalidate the results, or can they still be considered informative?
Also, am I missing any alternative framework to handle such low-recapture multi-session data?

Thank you very much in advance for any guidance!

Antonio Sampedro
Wildlife biologist | Tibetan Language Translator Research Officer at Himalayan Wolves Project
Mobile: +34 639843617 |
anton.s...@gmail.com
https://www.himalayanwolvesproject.org/

messages.subject: Re: Trap availability approach
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kirby, this is quite a challenging problem.  I think a general strategy would be to turn this challenge into a sensitivity analysis and essentially conduct the density estimation using several approaches.  At the end, the findings that are consistent across approaches are the ones most useful for inference (i.e., patterns in density, etc.).

Unfortunately, without a simulation it would be difficult to assess how exactly this lack of information would affect your density estimates.  The spatial patterns in availability will influence the effective detection probabilities and the realized density estimates.  Whether the induced noise is enough to degrade any important signals is tough to tell (though the sensitivity analysis could shed light).

Are these single-catch traps?  That is a general problem in SCR modeling with few straightforward solutions, though it has not stopped folks from simply listing the caveats and fitting models anyway.

messages.subject: Re: Question about oSCR minimum recaptures
messages.body_plain:
Hi Antonio, it's definitely frustrating when the data are so sparse.   How many spatial recaptures did you have?

There are not many solutions for wildlife monitoring when the data are lacking, aside from changing your design in some way.  Still, your estimates are certainly not the worst I've seen and the fact that the algorithm converged and gave you a result is a victory itself.  Sometimes a 30% CV is used as a general threshold for whether a population estimate is "robust", but that is certainly a gray area.  And again, this threshold would suggest a design change is needed for more robust monitoring but it would not stop folks from using the population estimate to make inferences (especially in the absence of alternatives).

messages.subject: ANNOUNCEMENT: ISEC 2027 in Mérida, México, January 8-15, 2027
messages.subject_clean: ANNOUNCEMENT: ISEC 2027 in Mérida, México, January 8-15, 2027
messages.body_plain:
Hello friends and colleagues,

Please see below the exciting news about ISEC27!

Chris

* I sometimes send emails out of hours; I do not expect others to do so.

Chris Sutherland (he/him/his)

Reader

Centre for Research into Ecological & Environmental Modelling

School of Mathematics and Statistics
University of St Andrews

W: website <https://www.sutherlandecology.com/>

E: cs...@st-andrews.ac.uk

From: ISEC Conference <isec.statist...@gmail.com>
Sent: 15 October 2025 04:01
To: ISEC Conference <isec.statist...@gmail.com>
Subject: ISEC 2027 in Mérida, México, January 8-15, 2027

(English:)

We are thrilled to announce that the next International Statistical Ecology Conference (ISEC) will be held in Mérida, México, on January 8-15, 2027, organized by the Autonomous University of Yucatán, and the Institute for Ecology and the Institute for Applied Mathematics and Systems Research from the National Autonomous University of México. ISEC is a biennial conference and serves as the main international gathering of statisticians and ecologists that work in the interdisciplinary field of statistical ecology. By closing the gap between ecology and statistics, two aims are achieved – helping ecologists discover new and state of the art statistical & machine learning methods and learn how best to use them, whilst at the same time make statisticians aware of the top priority methodological problems ecologists would like to solve.

The call for workshop proposals is now open. Previous 1-day and half-day workshops have covered R packages useful for the analysis of ecological data, animal movement modeling, generalized linear mixed models, generalized additive models, and Bayesian inference. We welcome similar workshop proposals that use R and/or Python, as well as those that focus on spatiotemporal models, eDNA, machine learning, artificial intelligence, computer vision, microbiome, and visualization of large data sets.

The call for roundtable proposals is also open. Roundtable discussions provide a platform to discuss important topics with other colleagues at ISEC. Some examples of possible roundtables: "The role of artificial intelligence in ecological data analysis", "Developing the statistical ecology community in México", "What topics should be included in a course on statistical ecology?".

The deadline for both is November 15, 2025, anywhere on Earth. For more information, visit statisticalecology.org <https://statisticalecology.org/>.

- Local Organizing Committee, ISEC 2027

(Español:)

Tenemos el agrado de anunciar que el próximo Congreso Internacional de Ecología Estadística (ISEC, por sus siglas en inglés) se llevará a cabo en Mérida, México, del 8 al 15 de enero de 2027. El evento será organizado por la Universidad Autónoma de Yucatán, en colaboración con el Instituto de Ecología y el Instituto de Investigaciones en Matemáticas Aplicadas y en Sistemas (IIMAS) de la Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México.

ISEC es un congreso bienal que funciona como el principal punto de encuentro internacional para estadísticos y ecólogos que trabajan en el campo interdisciplinario de la ecología estadística. Al cerrar la brecha entre la ecología y la estadística, se logran dos objetivos: ayudar a los ecólogos a descubrir métodos estadísticos y de aprendizaje automático (machine learning) nuevos y de vanguardia, y aprender cómo utilizarlos de la mejor manera posible; y, al mismo tiempo, hacer que los estadísticos conozcan los problemas metodológicos prioritarios que los ecólogos buscan resolver.

La convocatoria para propuestas de talleres ya está abierta. En años anteriores, se han ofrecido talleres de medio día o de un día completo sobre paqueterías de R útiles para el análisis de datos ecológicos, modelado de movimiento animal, modelos lineales generalizados mixtos, modelos aditivos generalizados e inferencia bayesiana. Se reciben con gusto propuestas de talleres similares que utilicen R y/o Python, así como aquellos que se enfoquen en modelos espaciotemporales, ADN ambiental (eDNA), aprendizaje automático, inteligencia artificial, visión por computadora, microbioma y visualización de grandes conjuntos de datos.

También está abierta la convocatoria para propuestas de mesas redondas. Las mesas redondas ofrecen un espacio para discutir temas importantes con otros colegas durante ISEC. Algunos ejemplos de posibles mesas redondas incluyen: “El papel de la inteligencia artificial en el análisis de datos ecológicos”, “Desarrollando la comunidad de ecología estadística en México”, “¿Qué temas deberían incluirse en un curso de ecología estadística?”.

La fecha límite para enviar propuestas para ambas convocatorias es el 15 de noviembre de 2025 (en cualquier lugar del mundo). Para más información, visita statisticalecology.org <https://statisticalecology.org/>

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,
Sorry in advance for the rather long message. I have several related questions, and I’d really appreciate your advice.
Our camera-trapping design is not a regular grid, but camera traps are placed at known marking sites that males frequently visit. I just wanted to mention this for completeness.

1. Our species has two male tactics that differ in home-range size and, consequently, in capture probabilities. Within each tactic, individuals can form groups. The territorial males, with smaller home ranges and higher capture rates, are more frequently found in small groups (typically 1–3 individuals), although such grouping can occasionally occur in the other tactic as well. Because these individuals move almost exclusively together, captures within a group are clearly not independent.
Would it be more appropriate to treat these groups as units rather than as individual animals?
Since our main focus is on density estimates, I assume that this would need to be accounted for in the final estimates, as otherwise densities would be underestimated if we treat a group as a unit/single animal.
For some of these group-living males, we also have telemetry data from multiple individuals within the same group.
What would be the best approach for handling this kind of structure and data in oSCR?

2. My second question concerns how much sampling effort can differ between sessions before it becomes problematic.
For example, if in one year the effective sampling effort per area was 30 days, while in another year it was 60 days, would this be acceptable as long as the difference in effort is properly reflected in the number of occasions?

3. I’d like to analyze four surveys conducted in different years, treating years as sessions. However, the areas with the camera traps were not identical across surveys. Only two areas were sampled in all four years, while the others were included in only one to three survey years.
Would it be possible to model all four years together, using years as sessions even though the sampled areas (partly) differ between years? Or would it be better to model each year separately, and additionally run an analysis restricted to the subset of areas sampled in all four years, treating years as sessions?

Thank you very much in advance for your time and any suggestions.

Best wishes,
Carlotta
